solution:
**Phylum Coelenterata / Cnidaria.**

The chapter pins both clues on the same phylum.

- **Diploblastic** - "In case of some animals, only two germ layers [Endoderm & ectoderm] are formed. Ex.: All Cnidarians." The phylum's own character list repeats it: "Body of these animals is radially symmetrical & diploblastic."
- **Acoelomate** - "Body cavity is absent in case of animals from phyla Porifera, Cnidaria and Platyhelminthes. Such animals are called as acoelomate."

Three phyla are acoelomate, but only one of the three is diploblastic. The chapter calls Platyhelminthes "triploblastic i.e. their body is made up of three germ layers- endoderm, ectoderm & mesoderm", and it never describes Porifera as diploblastic anywhere. So the two clues taken together leave Cnidaria alone.

Examples the chapter gives for the phylum: Hydra, Adamsia (Sea anemone), Physalia (Portuguese-man-of-war), Aurelia (Jelly fish) and Corals.

[Textbook note: this question turns on the phrase "water vascular system", and the chapter never uses it. A scan of all sixteen pages of the chapter finds that phrase only inside this question itself. The nearest thing the chapter says about the structure is that echinoderms "perform locomotion with the help of tube-feet. Tube feet are also useful for capturing the prey" - tube feet are the visible part of that system, but the system is never named or explained. This matters because without that outside term the chapter's other two clues also fit the jelly fish, which the chapter likewise calls radially symmetrical and prints as "Aurelia (Jelly fish)". The clue that actually decides the answer therefore comes from outside this chapter.]

**Star fish** (phylum Echinodermata).

What the chapter does support directly:

- **Radially symmetrical** - "Radial symmetry : In this type of body, if imaginary cut passes through central axis but any plane of body, it gives two equal halves. Ex. Star fish. In case of this animal, there are five different planes passing through central axis of body through which we can get two equal halves." The star fish is the chapter's own worked example of radial symmetry.
- **"Referred as fish though I am not"** - the chapter places Star fish in phylum Echinodermata, among the non-chordates. It is not in class Pisces and has no notochord, so despite its name it is not a fish at all.
- **Water vascular system** - the chapter's only related statement is that these animals move using tube-feet, which also capture prey.

The chapter's other Echinodermata characters fit the same animal: calcareous spines on the body, found only in the ocean, triploblastic and eucoelomate, a skeleton of calcareous spines and/or ossicles, and a good ability of regeneration.

**Phylum Aschelminthes.**

Each clue matches a character the chapter gives for this phylum.

- **"Thread like body"** - "Body of these animals is long thread-like or cylindrical. Hence, they are called as round worms."
- **Pseudocoelom** - "Body of these animals is triploblastic and pseudocoelomate." The criteria section explains what that means: "In case of animals from phylum Aschelminthes, they have body cavity but it is not formed by the above mentioned two ways. Hence those animals are called as pseudocoelomates."
- **"I live in your small intestine"** - "These animals are either free living or endoparasites", and the first example the chapter prints is "Ascaris (Intestinal worm)".

So the animal describing itself is Ascaris and the phylum is Aschelminthes. The other examples the chapter gives are Filarial worm and Loa loa (Eye worm).

**Phylum Porifera.**

The chapter states this case exactly: "In case of multicellular animals, if tissues are not formed, their body organization is called as 'Cellular grade organization'. Ex. Phylum-Porifera."

That is precisely the clue in the question - the animal is multicellular, yet no tissues are formed in its body.

The chapter's other characters for the phylum agree: "These animals are with simplest body plan and are called as 'Sponges'." They bear pores called ostia and oscula, most have an asymmetrical body, they have special collar cells, and they are sedentary, being always attached to a substratum. Examples: Sycon, Euspongia (Bath sponge), Hyalonema, Euplectella.

The chart the question refers to is the chapter's classification chart (figure 6.11), whose columns are Kingdom, Body organization, Body symmetry, Body cavity (Coelom) and Phylum. Reading each animal down those columns and then adding its own phylum or class characters:

| Animal | Classification | Characters the chapter gives |
|---|---|---|
| Bath sponge | Phylum Porifera (non-chordate) | Simplest body plan, called a sponge; bears pores - ostia and oscula; aquatic, most marine and a few fresh water; most have an asymmetrical body; has special collar cells; always attached to a substratum, hence sedentary and showing no locomotion; the spongy body is supported by spicules (calcium carbonate or silica) or spongin fibres; feeds on small organisms taken in with water through the ostia and given out through the oscula; reproduces by budding and/or sexually and regenerates well. Cellular grade organization - multicellular but with no tissues - and acoelomate. The chapter adds that the bath sponge is black and somewhat round, its body mainly of spongin fibres, giving it good water-holding capacity. |
| Grasshopper | Phylum Arthropoda (non-chordate) | Jointed appendages, which is what gives the phylum its name; body triploblastic, eucoelomate, bilaterally symmetrical and segmented; a chitinous exoskeleton around the body; unisexual. The chapter notes this is the largest phylum, found in all habitats from the deepest oceans to the highest mountains. |
| Rohu | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Pisces | Cold blooded (poikilotherm) and aquatic; spindle-shaped body to minimize water resistance; paired and unpaired fins, the tail fin acting as a steering organ; exoskeleton of scales and an endoskeleton either cartilaginous or bony; respiration by gills. Rohu is the first example the chapter prints for this class. |
| Penguin | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Aves | Completely adapted for aerial life; warm blooded (homeotherm), able to keep the body temperature constant; spindle-shaped body to minimize air resistance during flight; forelimbs modified into wings, digits covered with scales and bearing claws; exoskeleton in the form of feathers; neck present between head and trunk; jaws modified into a beak. |
| Frog | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Amphibia | Strictly aquatic during larval life with only aquatic respiration, while the adult lives in water as well as on land and can respire aquatically as well as aerially; two pairs of appendages with digits that bear no claws; exoskeleton absent, the skin without derivatives and usually kept moist for respiration; external ear absent but tympanum present; neck absent and eyes prominent with eyelids. |
| Lizard | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Reptilia | Described as the first true terrestrial animals, with creeping movement; cold blooded (poikilotherm); creeps because the body cannot be lifted up; skin dry and scaly; neck present between head and trunk; external ear absent; digits provided with claws. |
| Elephant | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Mammalia | Mammary glands present, which the chapter calls the typical character of the class; warm blooded; body divided into head, neck, trunk and tail; digits provided with nails, claws or hooves; exoskeleton in the form of hairs or fur. |
| Jellyfish | Phylum Coelenterata / Cnidaria (non-chordate) | Umbrella-like body, which the chapter calls a medusa (a cylindrical one is a polyp); mostly marine with only a few fresh water dwellers; radially symmetrical and diploblastic; cnidoblast-bearing tentacles around the mouth, the tentacles capturing prey while the cnidoblasts inject toxin, both also serving for protection. Cell-tissue grade organization and acoelomate. The chapter prints it as "Aurelia (Jelly fish)". |

**One animal is not in the chapter.** Seven of the eight are printed somewhere in the chapter's own example lists. **Grasshopper is not** - the Arthropoda examples are "Crab, spider, scorpion, millipede, centipede, cockroach, butterfly, honey bee, etc." Its characters above are therefore taken from the phylum's stated characters rather than from a printed example. It belongs in Arthropoda because it has jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton, and the chapter treats insects as members of this phylum when it asks why "only insects directly compete with humans for food".

The chapter traces the following progression.

**1. The artificial method.** "Greek philosopher Aristotle was the first to perform the animal classification. Aristotle classified the animals according to the criteria like body size, habits and habitats." The chapter calls this the "Artificial method" and records that it was also followed by Theophrastus, Pliny, John Ray and Linnaeus.

**2. The natural system of classification.** As sciences developed the references and therefore the criteria changed. "Natural system of classification was based on various criteria like body organization, types of cells, chromosomes, bio-chemical properties, etc."

**3. Classification based on evolution.** "By the time, system of classification based on evolution was also brought into practice. It was used by Dobzhansky and Meyer." The chapter adds that "Recently, Carl Woese has also proposed the animal classification."

**4. The traditional or conventional system.** "Traditionally, depending upon presence or absence of the notochord, the animal kingdom has been divided into two groups- Non-chordates and Chordates." The non-chordates were divided into ten phyla - Protozoa, Porifera, Coelenterata/Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata - while all chordates were grouped into the single phylum Chordata, itself divided into the sub-phyla Urochordata, Cephalochordata and Vertebrata.

**5. The new system, followed at present.** "At present, according to the five kingdom classification system of Robert Whittaker, all multicellular animals are included in Kingdom: Animalia. This system of classification is based upon some criteria like Body organization, Body symmetry, Body cavity, Germinal layers, Segmentation, etc."

**What changed between the last two stages** can be read off the chapter's two charts. In the conventional chart the kingdom is first split into the sub-kingdoms Non-chordates and Chordates, and Protozoa stands as the first of the ten non-chordate phyla. In the new chart the kingdom is defined as "Multicellular organisms without cell wall" and is divided directly into ten phyla - Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata and Chordata. So Chordata becomes one phylum among the ten rather than a separate sub-kingdom, and Protozoa no longer appears, the kingdom now being defined as multicellular.

**In short:** the criteria moved from external features that are easy to see (body size, habits, habitat) to internal and developmental ones (body organization, symmetry, germ layers, body cavity, segmentation), and the purpose moved from mere convenience of study towards showing the evolutionary relationship between animals - which is the third benefit the chapter lists for classification, that "It gives idea about animal evolution."

The two answer different questions about the same body.

**Grade of organization** asks **how far the cells of the body are built up into tissues, organs and organ systems**. It is a measure of structural complexity. The chapter gives these grades:

| Grade | What it means | Chapter's example |
|---|---|---|
| Protoplasmic grade | Unicellular, where "all the functions of life are performed by same cell" | Amoeba, Paramecium |
| Cellular grade | Multicellular, but tissues are not formed | Phylum Porifera |
| Cell-tissue grade | Cells come together to form tissues, "with the help of which all the body functions are performed" | Animals of phylum Cnidaria |
| Tissue-organ grade | "tissues are organized to form some organs. However, complete organ systems are not formed" | Flat worms |
| Organ-system grade | "different organs are joined together to form organ system that performs specific functions" | Crab, frog, human |

**Symmetry** asks **how the parts of the body are arranged about an imaginary axis** - whether an imaginary cut gives two equal halves, and through how many planes. The chapter gives:

| Type | What it means | Chapter's example |
|---|---|---|
| Asymmetrical body | "there is no any such imaginary axis of the body through which we can get two equal halves" | Some sponges |
| Radial symmetry | A cut through the central axis in any plane gives two equal halves | Star fish, which has five such planes |
| Bilateral symmetry | "there is only one such imaginary axis of body through which we can get two equal halves" | Insects, fishes, frog, birds, human |

**The exact difference.** Grade of organization is about the **level of construction** of the body - cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems. Symmetry is about the **geometrical arrangement** of the body about an axis. One describes how the body is built, the other describes how it is shaped.

**They are independent of each other**, which is why the chapter's classification chart uses "Body organization" and "Body symmetry" as two separate columns. For example, Cnidaria and Echinodermata are both radially symmetrical, yet Cnidaria stands only at cell-tissue grade while echinoderms fall under the chapter's rule that "Remaining all animals show 'Organ - system grade organization'". Equally, Porifera at cellular grade is asymmetrical while a frog at organ-system grade is bilaterally symmetrical. So knowing one tells you nothing about the other.

Following the chapter's own conventional classification chart:

| Rank | Name |
|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia |
| Sub-kingdom | Chordates |
| Phylum | Chordata |
| Sub-phylum | Vertebrata (Craniata) |
| Class | Pisces |

The chapter prints Shark among the examples of class Pisces: "Rohu, Pomfret, Sea horse, Shark, Electric ray, Sting ray, etc."

**Why each rank.** It is a chordate because its body is supported by a notochord, it has pharyngeal gill slits for respiration, its nerve cord is dorsal and hollow and its heart is ventral. It is placed in sub-phylum Vertebrata because there "notochord is replaced by vertebral column", the head is well developed and "Brain is protected by cranium". It is in class Pisces because it is a cold blooded (poikilotherm) aquatic animal with a spindle-shaped body, paired and unpaired fins, an exoskeleton of scales, an endoskeleton that is cartilaginous or bony, and respiration by gills.

The chapter lists seven characters for the phylum; four distinguishing ones are:

1. **Calcareous spines on the body.** "Calcareous spines are present on the body of these animals; hence they are called as echinoderms." The name of the phylum comes from this character.
2. **Exclusively marine.** "These animals are found only in ocean." No echinoderm is a fresh water or terrestrial animal.
3. **Symmetry that changes with age.** "Their body is triploblastic, eucoelomate. And it is radially symmetrical in adult stage. However, they show bilateral symmetry in larval stage." This difference between larva and adult is peculiar to the phylum.
4. **Locomotion by tube-feet.** "They perform locomotion with the help of tube-feet. Tube feet are also useful for capturing the prey. Some animals are sedentary."

The remaining three characters the chapter gives are that they have a skeleton made of calcareous spines and/or ossicles (plates), that they have a good ability of regeneration, and that they are mostly unisexual.

Examples: Star fish, sea-urchin, brittle star, sea-cucumber.

| Property | Butterfly | Bat |
|---|---|---|
| Phylum and class | Phylum Arthropoda - a non-chordate | Phylum Chordata, sub-phylum Vertebrata, class Mammalia - a chordate |
| Notochord / vertebral column | Notochord absent. The chapter's list of non-chordate characters begins "Body is not supported by rod-like notochord." | A vertebrate, in which "notochord is replaced by vertebral column" and the brain is protected by a cranium |
| Exoskeleton | "Chitinous exoskeleton is present around their body." | "Exoskeleton is in the form of hairs or fur." |
| Appendages | "These animals have jointed appendages. Hence they are called as arthropods." | "Digits are provided with nails, claws, or hooves." |
| Mammary glands and body temperature | Not a mammal, so no mammary glands. The chapter states nothing about the body temperature of arthropods. | "Presence of mammary glands is typical character of mammalia" and "These animals are warm blooded." |

Two further differences the chapter's two character lists give, if more are wanted: in a non-chordate the nerve cord, "if present, it is on ventral side. It is solid & paired" and the heart, if present, is dorsal; in a chordate the nerve cord is "present on dorsal side of body. It is hollow" and the heart is ventral.

**The point of the comparison:** both animals fly, but flight is not one of the criteria used in this classification. The chapter separates them on the notochord, which is the traditional criterion dividing non-chordates from chordates, and then on the characters of their respective phylum and class.

**Phylum Arthropoda.** The chapter prints cockroach among the phylum's examples: "Crab, spider, scorpion, millipede, centipede, cockroach, butterfly, honey bee, etc."

The scientific reasons, taken from the chapter's characters for the phylum:

1. **Jointed appendages.** "These animals have jointed appendages. Hence they are called as arthropods." A cockroach's legs and antennae are jointed.
2. **Body triploblastic, eucoelomate, bilaterally symmetrical and segmented.** The cockroach's body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen, which the chapter's figure of animals in phylum Arthropoda labels.
3. **Chitinous exoskeleton.** "Chitinous exoskeleton is present around their body."
4. **Unisexual.** "These animals are unisexual", the sexes being separate.

The chapter also notes that this is the largest phylum in the animal kingdom, with animals found in all types of habitats, and it groups the cockroach in its Arthropoda figure alongside the centipede, scorpion and butterfly.

**Because a class is decided by structural characters, not by habitat** - and on every character the chapter gives, the tortoise matches Reptilia and not Amphibia. The chapter prints Tortoise among the examples of class Reptilia: "Tortoise, Lizard, Snake, etc."

| Character | Class Amphibia | Tortoise, in class Reptilia |
|---|---|---|
| Skin | "Exoskeleton is absent. Skin is without any derivative and usually kept moist for respiration." | "Their skin is dry and scaly." |
| Digits | "Digits are without claws." | "Digits are provided with claws." |
| Neck | "Neck is absent." | "Neck is present between head & trunk." |
| Larval life | "These animals are strictly aquatic during larval life and perform only aquatic respiration." | The chapter describes reptiles as "first true terrestrial animals with creeping movement" and records no aquatic larval stage for them. |

A tortoise has dry scaly skin instead of moist glandular skin, clawed digits instead of clawless ones, and a distinct neck where an amphibian has none. Living partly in water is therefore not enough to make it an amphibian - the amphibian condition is a moist skin used for respiration and an obligatory aquatic larval stage, and the tortoise has neither. It is accordingly placed in class Reptilia.

The jelly fish, which the chapter prints as "Aurelia (Jelly fish)", belongs to phylum Coelenterata / Cnidaria, and the chapter gives that phylum this character:

"Cnidoblast bearing tentacles are present around the mouth. Tentacles are useful for capturing the prey whereas cnidoblasts inject the toxin in the body of prey. Those are useful for protection too."

So the tentacles that surround the mouth of a jelly fish carry stinging cells called **cnidoblasts**. When our body comes into contact with the animal, those cnidoblasts discharge and **inject their toxin into our skin**, exactly as they would into a prey animal. The chapter adds that these same structures also serve the animal for protection, so the reaction is triggered by contact rather than only by the animal feeding.

It is this injected toxin that causes the burning and irritation of the skin.

Because the chapter makes Vertebrata a **part** of Chordata, not another name for it:

"All chordate animals are grouped together in a single phylum and the name of phylum is same i.e. Phylum- Chordata. This phylum has been divided into three subphyla as- Urochordata, Cephalochordata & Vertebrata."

**All vertebrates are chordates.** Every vertebrate lies inside sub-phylum Vertebrata, which lies inside phylum Chordata. So a vertebrate necessarily has the chordate characters - a notochord at some stage, pharyngeal gill slits at some stage, a single hollow dorsal nerve cord and a ventral heart.

**But all chordates are not vertebrates.** Vertebrata is only one of the three sub-phyla. The other two are also chordates and have no vertebral column at all:

- **Urochordata** - marine animals whose body is covered by a test or tunic, in which "notochord is present in only tail region of larvae". Examples: Herdmania, Doliolum, Oikopleura.
- **Cephalochordata** - small fish-like marine animals in which "Notochord is present throughout the body length". Example: Amphioxus.

In Vertebrata alone "notochord is replaced by vertebral column"; the animals of the other two sub-phyla keep a notochord and never form a backbone. Hence every vertebrate is a chordate, while the members of Urochordata and Cephalochordata are chordates that are not vertebrates.

The chapter states this directly: "Through the view point of evolution, Balanoglossus is considered as connecting link between non-chordates and chordates. This animal shows the characters of both the groups."

The characters of the two groups that it shares, from the chapter's own lists:

**Chordate characters it shows.** "Notochord is present in proboscis region only" and "They have one to many pharyngeal gill slits." The chapter's list of chordate characters begins "Body is supported by notochord" and "Pharyngeal gill-slits or lungs are present for respiration", so on both counts Balanoglossus shows a chordate feature.

**Non-chordate placement.** Balanoglossus belongs to phylum Hemichordata, which the chapter counts as the tenth of the ten **non-chordate** phyla in the conventional system. Its notochord is confined to the proboscis instead of running the length of the body, which is exactly why the chapter says "Hence, they are called as hemichordates" - half-chordates.

An animal that carries a partial notochord and pharyngeal gill slits like a chordate, while being classified among the non-chordates, stands between the two groups. That is what makes it their connecting link.

Because a reptile is a **poikilotherm**. The chapter's list of characters for class Reptilia says: "These are cold blooded (poikilotherms) animals."

The chapter defines the opposite condition where it describes class Aves: "These are warm blooded (Homeotherms) i.e. they can maintain their body temperature constant." Keeping the body temperature constant is therefore the property of a homeotherm.

A reptile is not a homeotherm, so it does not have that ability, and its body temperature does not remain constant. This is also why the chapter can use the single word "Poikilotherms" as a character in its own right in the exercise chart.

[The chapter defines poikilothermy only as being cold blooded, and by contrast with the homeotherm's constant temperature. It does not state in so many words that a reptile's body temperature follows the temperature of its surroundings, so that step is not claimed here.]

| Body cavity | Germ Layer | Phylum |
|---|---|---|
| Absent | not formed - see the note below | Porifera |
| Absent | Triploblastic | **Platyhelminthes** |
| Pseudocoelom | **Triploblastic** | Aschelminthes |
| Present | **Triploblastic** | Arthropoda |

**Row 2 - the phylum is Platyhelminthes.** The chapter names exactly three acoelomate phyla: "Body cavity is absent in case of animals from phyla Porifera, Cnidaria and Platyhelminthes." Of those three, the one the chapter calls triploblastic is Platyhelminthes - "These are triploblastic i.e. their body is made up of three germ layers- endoderm, ectoderm & mesoderm." Cnidaria is diploblastic, and the chapter gives Porifera no germ-layer description at all, so Platyhelminthes is the only phylum that is both acoelomate and triploblastic.

**Row 3 - Triploblastic.** Aschelminthes character 3: "Body of these animals is triploblastic and pseudocoelomate."

**Row 4 - Triploblastic.** Arthropoda character 4: "Body of these animals is triploblastic, eucoelomate, bilaterally symmetrical and segmented." The chapter's rule for row 4's body cavity is that a true cavity "is present in animals of phylum Annelida and all phyla coming after Annelida", which includes Arthropoda.

**Row 1 - the chapter does not assign a germ layer to Porifera, and that is worth saying rather than filling in.** Its germ-layer section names only two categories - "In case of some animals, only two germ layers [Endoderm & ectoderm] are formed. Ex.: All Cnidarians. In most of all the remaining animals, three germ layers are formed" - and it never applies either label to Porifera. The eight characters it lists for the phylum say nothing about germ layers either.

What the chapter does give is the reasoning: germ layers are what tissues arise from, since "from those germ layers only, different tissues are formed in the body"; and a sponge has no tissues at all, since "if tissues are not formed, their body organization is called as 'Cellular grade organization'. Ex. Phylum-Porifera." Read together, those two statements mean that germ layers are not formed in Porifera. So the honest entry for this cell is **absent / not formed** - neither diploblastic nor triploblastic, both of which the chapter withholds from this phylum.

| Type | Character | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclostomata | **Jaw-less mouth provided with a sucker** | **Petromyzon** |
| **Pisces** | Gill respiration | **Rohu** |
| Amphibia | **Larva strictly aquatic with only aquatic respiration; the adult lives in water as well as on land and respires aquatically as well as aerially** | **Frog** |
| **Mammalia** | **Presence of mammary glands; warm blooded** | Whale |
| **Reptilia** | Poikilotherms | **Tortoise** |

"Type" here means a class of sub-phylum Vertebrata. The chapter names six - Cyclostomata, Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia - and the chart has five rows, so one class (Aves) is not used.

- **Cyclostomata.** Character 1 of the class is "These animals have jaw-less mouth provided with sucker." Examples printed: Petromyzon, Myxine. Its other characters are a soft skin without any scale, absent paired appendages, a cartilaginous endoskeleton, and that most are ectoparasites.
- **Gill respiration gives Pisces.** Character 5 of class Pisces is "Respiration occurs with gills." Examples printed: Rohu, Pomfret, Sea horse, Shark, Electric ray, Sting ray.
- **Amphibia.** Character 1 of the class is the one entered above. Examples printed: Frog, Toad, Salamander.
- **Poikilotherms gives Reptilia.** Character 2 of Reptilia is "These are cold blooded (poikilotherms) animals." Examples printed: Tortoise, Lizard, Snake. Note that the chapter applies the same word to Pisces as well, whose character 1 is "These are cold blooded (Poikilotherms) aquatic animals" - so taken alone the word fits two classes. Reptilia is the class that fits this row because the Pisces row is already used by gill respiration.
- **Whale gives Mammalia.** The typical character of the class is "Presence of mammary glands is typical character of mammalia", and "These animals are warm blooded." A whale is placed here for those characters and not for its habitat, since class is decided by structure rather than by where an animal lives.

**A gap worth naming.** The chapter does not print whale among its Mammalia examples, which are "Elephant, Human, Kangaroo, Dolphin, Bat, etc." It raises the animal only in a "Use your brain power" box - "Animals like whale, walrus live in water (ocean). Whether they are included in pisces or mammalia?" - and leaves that question for the student rather than answering it. The entry above is therefore reached from the class's stated characters, and is supported by the chapter listing Dolphin, an equally aquatic mammal, in this class.

Eight of the twelve are non-chordates and four are chordates, all four falling in sub-phylum Vertebrata.

For the sketch and labels, use the chapter's own labelled figures for each phylum and class as the model - it labels a sponge, a jelly fish, Planaria, Ascaris, an earthworm, a cockroach and butterfly, an octopus, a star fish, a fish, a frog, a wall lizard and a pigeon.

[Textbook note: this question cannot be answered from its printed text. The book prints only the one-line instruction "Label the following." beside four unlabelled drawings of animals, and the whole content of the question is in those drawings. They are not reproduced in this record, so the four animals are deliberately not named here - identifying them from a description would be a guess rather than the book's content. Work from the printed page.]

**What the question asks you to do.** Write the names of the parts onto each drawing, in the way the chapter's own figures are labelled. Find the figure in the chapter that matches each drawing in front of you and copy its labels onto your sketch.

The labels the chapter itself uses, which are the ones expected here, include:

- **Sponge (Sycon)** - ostium, outlet (oscula), collar cells, amoebocyte, spicule, non-living part.
- **Hydra** - mouth, tentacles, body, new bud, ovary, testes.
- **Jelly fish** - bell, tentacle, oral arms, mouth, muscle ring, tube, gonads, intestine.
- **Planaria** - mouth, pharynx, eye spot, nerve chord, ganglia, gastrovascular cavity.
- **Ascaris** - mouth, genital aperture, anus, tail.
- **Liver fluke and tape worm** - oral sucker, ventral sucker, leaf like body, excretory pore, genital aperture.
- **Earthworm, leech and Nereis** - mouth, anus, segment, clitellum, tentacle, parapodia.
- **Cockroach** - head, thorax, abdomen, antennae, legs, wings.
- **Octopus and snail** - eye, tentacle, sucker, siphon, foot.
- **Balanoglossus** - proboscis, collar, trunk.
- **Fish** - mouth, eye, gill slits, lateral line, dorsal fin, pectoral fin, pelvic fin, ventral fin, caudal fin.
- **Frog and toad** - nares, fore arm, leg, trunk, tympanum, skin.
- **Pigeon** - beak, eyes, neck, head, claws, legs.
- **Bat** - patagium, body, eyes.
